ukmt-cayley-2022-c1.title: Forced divisions
ukmt-cayley-2022-c1.body:
Each number must be divisible by the number it is divided by. Find the forced pairings, starting with the divisors that have few multiples in $62,\dots,70$.

- Multiples of $9$: only $63$. So $63\div9=7$.
- Multiples of $8$: only $64$. So $64\div8=8$.
- Multiples of $7$: $63,70$; $63$ is used, so $70\div7=10$.
- Multiples of $6$: only $66$ (as $60$ and $72$ are out of range). So $66\div6=11$.
- Multiples of $5$: $65,70$; $70$ is used, so $65\div5=13$.
- Multiples of $4$: $64,68$; $64$ is used, so $68\div4=17$.
- Multiples of $3$: $63,66,69$; only $69$ is left, so $69\div3=23$.
- Multiples of $2$: of the remaining $62,67$ only $62$ qualifies, so $62\div2=31$.
- Finally $67\div1=67$.

The pairing is forced, so $S$ has exactly one possible value:
$$S=7+8+10+11+13+17+23+31+67=187 .$$

**Answer: $S=187$ is the only possible value.**

ukmt-cayley-2022-c2.title: Use divisibility by $5$ and $9$
ukmt-cayley-2022-c2.body:
A six-digit palindrome has the form $\overline{abccba}$ with $a\ne0$.

$45=5\cdot9$. Divisible by $5$ means the last digit $a$ is $0$ or $5$; since $a\ne0$, $a=5$.

Divisible by $9$ means the digit sum $2(5+b+c)$ is a multiple of $9$. As $\gcd(2,9)=1$, $5+b+c$ must be a multiple of $9$. Since $5\le5+b+c\le23$, we need $5+b+c\in\{9,18\}$, i.e. $b+c=4$ or $b+c=13$.

- $b+c=4$: $(b,c)=(0,4),(1,3),(2,2),(3,1),(4,0)$, giving $504405,\ 513315,\ 522225,\ 531135,\ 540045$.
- $b+c=13$: $(b,c)=(4,9),(5,8),(6,7),(7,6),(8,5),(9,4)$, giving $549945,\ 558855,\ 567765,\ 576675,\ 585585,\ 594495$.

All eleven are palindromes ending in $5$ whose digit sum $2(5+b+c)$ is $18$ or $36$, so each is divisible by $5$ and by $9$, hence by $45$.

**Answer: the eleven numbers listed above.** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2022-c3.title: Column addition
ukmt-cayley-2022-c3.body:
The equation says $\overline{abcd}+\overline{efgh}=10000$. Add column by column.

- Units: $d+h$ ends in $0$ and $2\le d+h\le16$, so $d+h=10$ with a carry of $1$.
- Tens: $c+g+1$ ends in $0$ and $3\le c+g+1\le17$, so $c+g+1=10$: $c+g=9$, carry $1$.
- Hundreds: similarly $b+f=9$, carry $1$.
- Thousands: $a+e+1=10$, so $a+e=9$.

**(a)** If all eight letters are different digits from $1$ to $8$, they are exactly $1,2,\dots,8$, with sum $36$. But the equations give a sum of
$$(d+h)+(c+g)+(b+f)+(a+e)=10+9+9+9=37\ne36 .$$
Contradiction, so there are no solutions.

**(b)** Conversely any choice of digits $1$ to $8$ with $d+h=10$ and $c+g=b+f=a+e=9$ is a solution.

- $(d,h)$: $d$ can be $2,\dots,8$ and $h=10-d$ (also in $2..8$): $7$ choices.
- Each of $(c,g),(b,f),(a,e)$: the first digit is any of $1,\dots,8$ and the second is $9$ minus it: $8$ choices each.

That gives $7\cdot8^3=3584$ ordered pairs of numbers. The two numbers are never equal (equal numbers would each be $0.5000$, which contains a $0$), so each solution is counted exactly twice. Hence the number of solutions is
$$\frac{7\cdot8^3}2=7\cdot2^8=1792 .$$

**Answer: (a) no solutions; (b) $1792=7\cdot2^8$.** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2022-c4.title: Central angles
ukmt-cayley-2022-c4.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of the circle. The octagon's vertices are $45^\circ$ apart as seen from $O$, so $\angle AOD=3\times45^\circ=135^\circ$ (going $A\to B\to C\to D$).

In the equilateral triangle $APQ$ each side subtends an inscribed angle of $60^\circ$ at the opposite vertex, hence a central angle of $120^\circ$. So $\angle AOP=120^\circ$, and $P$ (between $C$ at $90^\circ$ and $D$ at $135^\circ$) is $120^\circ$ from $A$.

Therefore
$$\angle POD=135^\circ-120^\circ=15^\circ .$$
A chord subtending $15^\circ$ at the centre is a side of the regular polygon with $360^\circ/15^\circ=24$ sides.

**Answer: $n=24$**

ukmt-cayley-2022-c5.title: Construct every integer
ukmt-cayley-2022-c5.body:
We show every integer $k$ occurs as a solution.

Take $a=2$, $b=1-k$, $c=1+k$. These are integers, $a\ne0$, and $a=b+c$ (so one of the three is the sum of the other two). The equation $2x+(1-k)=1+k$ gives $2x=2k$, i.e. $x=k$.

So any integer $k$ can be the value of $x$, and nothing else needs to be checked: the set of possible integer values is all integers.

(For comparison: if $c=a+b$ the equation forces $x=1$, and if $b=a+c$ it forces $x=-1$; the case $a=b+c$ is what yields every other integer.)

**Answer: every integer.** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2022-c6.title: Grid of colours and labels
ukmt-cayley-2022-c6.body:
Put the nine stones in a $3\times3$ table: rows are the colours (blue, red, yellow) and columns are the labels ($1,2,3$). A tower is three different cells with an order (bottom, middle, top).

The three stones avoid a set exactly when

- not all three are in the same row (colour) and not all three in different rows: so they occupy **exactly two rows**, and
- not all three in the same column and not all three in different columns: so they occupy **exactly two columns**.

Choose the two rows ($3$ ways) and the two columns ($3$ ways). These give a $2\times2$ block of $4$ cells; any three of its cells occupy both rows and both columns, so every choice of $3$ out of the $4$ cells works: $4$ ways. Conversely every good triple lies in exactly one such block.

So there are $3\cdot3\cdot4=36$ good sets of stones, and each can be stacked in $3!=6$ orders:
$$36\times6=216 .$$

**Answer: $216$**
